messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Koa is a 45-year-old chef from the Pacific Islands, now working the dinner line at a busy downtown restaurant. Two years ago, after a late shift, a fellow cook he had trusted followed him into the walk-in cooler and raped him. Koa managed to get free and drove home, but he never reported it. He told himself it was a freak incident, something he could lock away. He could describe what happened easily enough—the cold air, the sound of the latch clicking shut, the weight of the other man’s body—but he could never put those moments in the right order. He would start telling someone about the assailant’s voice, then jump to the drive home, then realize he had skipped the most horrifying part. And then, just as he felt the scene coming back fully, his mind would clamp down, and the memory would vanish, leaving him hollow and drained.

In the months that followed, Koa’s belief about himself shifted in ways he had not anticipated. He had always been defined by his hands—his speed with a knife, his instinct for seasoning, his ability to hold a hot pan steady. Now he felt those hands were dirty. Even after three showers, he could still smell the floor of the cooler on his skin. The contamination clung to him like a second layer, and he began to believe that his life was over. He had already been divorced before the assault; now he was certain he would never be close to anyone again. Who would want to be near something so soiled? The moment he let himself think about the rape, that feeling of contamination surged, and he would push the memory away before it could fully surface—leaving the sequence even more tangled the next time it returned.

Working as a chef became a daily minefield. Every time he stepped into the walk-in cooler to grab produce, his heart hammered and his mind went blank. He would grab a crate of onions and flee, unable to recall the order of what he had just seen in his thoughts. His hands shook on the knife handles. He started leaving cuts on the line, missing steps in recipes, and his sous chef noticed. Koa told himself he was no longer capable of the precise work that had once defined him. That appraisal made him even more desperate to avoid thinking about the event, so he shoved the memories aside harder, which only made the flashbacks more disorganized and harder to dismiss when they finally broke through.

He took to arriving early to the kitchen to have the cooler already stocked, so he did not have to go inside. He stopped working late shifts. His boss questioned his reliability, and Koa felt a fresh wave of shame. The belief that his life was destroyed grew stronger every time he failed at a task he had once done effortlessly. And each time he tried to recount the trauma to a therapist or a friend, he found himself stuck in the same loop: he could talk about the event as if it were a story he had memorized, but the order was wrong, and before he reached the worst part—the moment the latch clicked—he would choke it off, leaving the memory incomplete. That incompleteness only confirmed to him that he could never master what had happened, that he was permanently broken.

Last month, after burning his arm on a hot range because he was dissociating through a recall, Koa finally called a trauma clinic. He is terrified that he will never cook again, but more than that, he is exhausted by the cycle: the feeling of dirtiness that drives the memory away, and the memory that returns in a confused rush, cementing his conviction that his life is over. He hopes someone can help him hold the whole story still long enough to see it through.
